text: You're given n nodes labeled zero to n minus one, and a list of undirected edges. Return true if these edges form a valid tree.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — a valid tree means the graph is fully connected and has no cycle. Equivalently, it has exactly n minus one edges and is connected. Is that right?
Two quick edge cases. A single node with no edges is a valid tree. And are there duplicate edges or self-loops?

Let me run through the examples. Five nodes, with edges zero-one, zero-two, zero-three, one-four — four edges, all connected, no cycle, so true. But zero-one, one-two, two-three, one-three, one-four is five edges for five nodes; that's one too many, so there's a cycle, and the answer is false.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. I need to check connectivity and acyclicity together. This problem reminds me of Union-Find, the cleanest fit for incremental connectivity: I merge the two endpoints of each edge, and if an edge ever connects two nodes already in the same set, that's a cycle. Combined with the n minus one edge-count check, that decides it. Each operation is near constant time with path compression and union by size. A DFS from node zero, checking that it visits all n nodes and never revisits a non-parent, also works, but Union-Find generalizes nicely to counting components too.

Here's the plan. One: if the edge count isn't n minus one, return false right away. Two: start every node as its own root, and union the endpoints of each edge, counting the merges that succeed. Three: return true only if there were exactly n minus one successful merges. One thing worth flagging — I pack the size into the same parent array using a negative value, so a root stores minus its size and no separate array is needed. And on the union, I attach the smaller tree under the larger and add the sizes, which keeps the trees shallow. Together with path compression in find, that's the near-constant amortized cost. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. I'll think out loud as I go. Find returns x if its parent value is negative, otherwise it recurses to the root. Union finds both roots; if they match, it returns false, because this edge would close a cycle. Otherwise it makes root X the bigger tree, adds the two negative sizes, and hangs root Y under root X. The main function guards the edge count, fills parent with minus one, and counts successful unions. One thing worth flagging — the find line does path compression inline: parent of x equals find of parent of x reassigns every node on the path to point straight at the root.

Let's dry-run the code on five nodes, edges zero-one, zero-two, zero-three, one-four. The count is four, which is n minus one, so we proceed. Each union attaches a fresh node to root zero, whose value grows from minus two to minus five. The row that matters is one-four: find of one is already zero, so four hangs under zero, and add reaches four — true. Now the cycle case: four nodes, edges zero-one, one-two, two-zero. The count check passes, but the third edge finds two and zero under the same root, so union returns false. Add stalls at two, below three, so false. Correct.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is O of E times alpha of n, effectively linear in the edges — the inverse-Ackermann factor is at most about four for any practical n. Space is O of n for the single parent array. Oh, one more thing — this same structure answers a whole family of problems: drop the n minus one guard and count roots, and you get the number of connected components; keep merging as edges stream in, and you have online cycle detection for a growing graph.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You nailed the tree definition as n minus one edges and connected, and mapped it to Union-Find. You explained the negative-size packing and union by size clearly. And you showed the cycle case where a same-root edge stops the count. Good work.
